primer.byz_p_world.title: Empire of the Romans
primer.byz_p_world.text: You were born in the empire of the Romans – that is what its people call themselves: Rhomaioi, Romans. The word "Byzantium" will be coined by scholars centuries later. The ruler is the basileus, an emperor seen as chosen by God; there is no law of succession, and generals and courtiers have seized the throne more than once. The capital is Constantinople, simply "the City"; the language is Greek, yet the laws are still called Roman. Neighbours call the Romans Greeks, and the Slavs call their capital Tsargrad, "the Emperor's City".
primer.byz_p_world_amorian.title: The icons return
primer.byz_p_world_amorian.text: On the throne sits young Michael III of the Amorian dynasty; at first his mother, Empress Theodora, ruled for him. In 843 she restored the icons to the churches for good, ending a quarrel that had split the empire for over a century – the day is still kept as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. Patriarch Photios is the most learned man of his age, and in 863 the brothers Cyril and Methodius of Thessalonica set out for the Slavs of Moravia with an alphabet for their tongue. In 860 the boats of the Rus first appeared beneath the City's walls.
primer.byz_p_world_macedon.title: The Macedonian dynasty
primer.byz_p_world_macedon.text: The empire is on the rise. In 867 Basil I, a former groom of peasant stock, founded the Macedonian dynasty, which rules for almost two centuries. The Romans retake Crete (961) and Antioch (969) from the Arabs, and Basil II, called the Bulgar-Slayer, has conquered Bulgaria by 1018. Once more the empire stretches from the Danube to the Euphrates, and the gold nomisma is prized from Italy to Baghdad. In 988 Prince Vladimir of Kiev was baptised too, marrying Basil II's sister, the princess Anna.
primer.byz_p_world_crisis.title: Years of turmoil
primer.byz_p_world_crisis.text: The Macedonian line has died out, and generals and courtiers take the throne one after another. In 1071 at Manzikert the Seljuks crushed the Roman army, and Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes was captured by Sultan Alp Arslan. While the capital quarrels over power, the Turks overrun Asia Minor – the empire's granary and its main source of soldiers. That same year the Normans took Bari, the last Roman city in Italy, and the gold nomisma is losing weight and shine.
primer.byz_p_world_komnenoi.title: The Komnenoi
primer.byz_p_world_komnenoi.text: This is the age of the Komnenoi. Alexios I Komnenos took the throne in 1081 and saved the empire: he beat back the Normans and the Pechenegs and called on the West for help against the Turks – in 1096–1097 thousands of crusaders marched through Constantinople. His son John II and grandson Manuel I won back parts of Asia Minor and kept a dazzling court. But the wealth of Italian merchants angers the townsfolk, and after 1185, under the Angeloi, the empire weakens in strife and the Bulgarians break away again.
primer.byz_p_world_latin.title: The City in Latin hands
primer.byz_p_world_latin.text: In April 1204 the knights of the Fourth Crusade and the Venetians stormed Constantinople and plundered it for three days. The bronze horses of the Hippodrome were shipped to Venice; a Latin emperor sits in the City, and a Catholic patriarch serves in Hagia Sophia. The united empire of the Romans is gone – only its fragments remain: the Empire of Nicaea under the Laskarids, Epirus and Trebizond. Many townsfolk have fled; those who stayed pray in their own churches under Frankish rule and wait for the day the City is theirs again.
primer.byz_p_world_nicaea_exile.title: Capital in exile
primer.byz_p_world_nicaea_exile.text: Your city has become the capital of the Romans in exile. After 1204 the patriarch, scholars and nobles fled here from captured Constantinople, and Theodore I Laskaris was crowned emperor here. His son-in-law John III Vatatzes (1221–1254) rules so thriftily that, according to the historian Nikephoros Gregoras, he bought his wife a crown with money from selling eggs from his own poultry yards. The court often stays at nearby Nymphaion, and Nicaea gathers strength to win back the City.
primer.byz_p_world_trebizond.title: Empire of the Grand Komnenoi
primer.byz_p_world_trebizond.text: In 1204, around the time Constantinople fell, two grandsons of Emperor Andronikos I – Alexios and David Komnenos – seized Trebizond with the help of Queen Tamar of Georgia. Ever since, there has been a small empire of the Grand Komnenoi here. It lives on trade: silk and spices from Tabriz pass through the city, and the Genoese and Venetians keep their trading posts. To buy peace, the emperors marry their daughters – famous beauties – to Turkmen beys and Georgian kings.
primer.byz_p_world_palaiologoi.title: The City regained
primer.byz_p_world_palaiologoi.text: On 25 July 1261 a Nicaean force under the general Alexios Strategopoulos slipped into Constantinople almost without a fight, and Michael VIII Palaiologos gave the City back to the Romans. But the empire is not what it was: Turkish beys, among them Osman, take Asia Minor piece by piece, and the Genoese of Galata across the Golden Horn take its trade. Catalan mercenaries hired against the Turks plunder Thrace themselves, and from 1321 grandfather and grandson, the two Andronikoi, fight each other for the throne.
primer.byz_p_world_decline.title: An empire in decline
primer.byz_p_world_decline.text: Hard times. In 1341–1347 John Kantakouzenos wars against the regents of young John V, and both sides call in Serbs and Turks. In 1347 the Black Death reached the City, and in 1354 an earthquake toppled the walls of Gallipoli and the Ottomans gained a foothold in Europe. Soon Adrianople becomes their capital, and Emperor John V travels to Rome and Venice to beg for help – and comes home empty-handed. The empire has shrunk to the City, Thessalonica and the Morea.
primer.byz_p_world_last.title: The last decades
primer.byz_p_world_last.text: All that remains is Constantinople, a few islands and the Morea in the Peloponnese, with the sultan's lands on every side. In 1394–1402 Bayezid I besieged the City, which was saved only when Timur crushed the Ottomans at Ankara. Emperor Manuel II toured Europe begging for help, and his son John VIII signed a union with Rome at Florence in 1439 – many Romans never accepted it. "Better the Turkish turban than the Latin mitre," say the union's opponents.
primer.byz_p_world_fall.title: The City has fallen
primer.byz_p_world_fall.text: On 29 May 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II took Constantinople after a siege of nearly two months; the last emperor, Constantine XI, died on the walls. The City became the sultans' capital and Hagia Sophia a mosque. Yet the Romans have not vanished: the sultan made Patriarch Gennadios Scholarios head of all his Orthodox subjects, and the Greeks go on living, trading and praying in their churches – now under foreign rule.
primer.byz_p_society.title: A ladder of ranks
primer.byz_p_society.text: At the top are the basileus and his court: hundreds of officials with titles such as protospatharios or magistros, each receiving a yearly roga from the emperor – a salary in gold and silk. Below them come the provincial "powerful", the dynatoi, with their estates, then merchants and guild masters of the City, peasants, and at the very bottom slaves. But the ladder is not closed: everyone remembers that the peasant's son Basil I became emperor, and learning and service can lift a person very high.
primer.byz_p_society_slave.title: Someone else's property
primer.byz_p_society_slave.text: You were born in a house where your parents belong to someone. The Romans own fewer slaves than ancient Rome did: they are mostly captives – Slavs, Bulgarians, Arabs, later Rus and Tatars from the Black Sea markets. They serve in noble houses, kitchens and workshops, more rarely in the fields. The Church counts freeing a slave as a good deed, and many masters free their servants in their wills; in 1095 Emperor Alexios I ordered that slaves' marriages be blessed in church just like those of free people.
primer.byz_p_society_peasant.title: Peasants of the theme
primer.byz_p_society_peasant.text: Your family are peasants of a theme, a military province governed by a strategos. You live in a village, a chorion, and the whole village answers for its taxes together: if a neighbour runs away, his share is spread among the rest. Besides the land tax there is the kapnikon, the "smoke tax" on every hearth, plus road work and feeding passing soldiers. More and more villages fall to great landlords – the dynatoi and the monasteries – and then the peasants become paroikoi, dependent tenants on someone else's land.
primer.byz_p_society_noble.title: Among the powerful
primer.byz_p_society_noble.text: Your family belongs to those the Romans call the "powerful", the dynatoi. You have estates worked by paroikoi, a house with a marble courtyard, and the men hold court titles: each title means a badge on one's robe, a place in ceremonies, and the roga, a salary the basileus hands out in person before Easter. The great families – the Phokades, Skleroi, Doukai, Komnenoi, later the Kantakouzenoi – intermarry, feud and plot. A fall can be as swift as a rise: those in disgrace are forced to take monastic vows.
primer.byz_p_birth.title: Name and baptism
primer.byz_p_birth.text: Roman babies are delivered by a midwife, the maia, and on the eighth day a priest says the prayer for naming the child – often after a saint or a grandparent. Baptism usually comes around the fortieth day, when the mother, after a prayer of purification, may enter the church again. The godparent becomes spiritual kin to the family: their children may never marry yours. Against Gylou – a she-demon believed to kill infants – amulets hang over the cradle, though priests grumble at such superstitions.
primer.byz_p_childhood.title: Raising children
primer.byz_p_childhood.text: Babies are swaddled tight "so the legs grow straight", and they are nursed by the mother or a hired wet nurse – in noble houses she becomes almost one of the family. Children play with knucklebones, balls, wooden horses and clay dolls. From six or seven, if there is money, boys are sent to a schoolmaster to read the Psalter, while girls learn to spin, weave and keep house. Peasant children are herding geese and goats by the age of seven.
primer.byz_p_home.title: House and home
primer.byz_p_home.text: Constantinople is crowded: two- and three-storey houses of brick and timber lean their balconies over the streets, and an old law of Emperor Zeno forbids building closer than 12 feet to a neighbour or blocking his view of the sea. A rich house has an inner courtyard with a well, a mosaic floor and a bath. Peasants live in one or two rooms of stone or mud brick, often above the animals' stall. Light comes from oil lamps, warmth from charcoal braziers, and an icon always hangs in the corner.
primer.byz_p_food.title: Bread, fish and fasting
primer.byz_p_food.text: The Romans eat bread – white for the rich, barley for the poor – beans, greens, olives, sheep's cheese and plenty of fish. The favourite seasoning is garos, a fermented fish sauce, and wine is often treated with resin to keep: the Western envoy Liutprand complained in 968 that it tasted of pitch. It is drunk mixed with water, and warm in winter. On nearly half the days of the year – Wednesdays, Fridays and the four great fasts – meat is forbidden.
primer.byz_p_clothes.title: Silk and purple
primer.byz_p_clothes.text: Clothing shows rank. Men wear a long tunic with a cloak over it; the rich wear silk woven with eagles and griffins, the rest wool and linen. Purple dye from sea snails and certain silks are reserved for the imperial court: the Book of the Eparch forbids merchants to sell them to foreigners. Women cover their hair and wear long dresses with wide sleeves – noblewomen with pearls and gold embroidery – while peasants go about in coarse wool and leather sandals.
primer.byz_p_faith.title: An Orthodox empire
primer.byz_p_faith.text: The faith of the Romans is Orthodoxy, and the church is the heart of life. Since 843, when the icons were restored for good, every home has a corner with an icon and a little oil lamp. Legend says that Prince Vladimir's envoys, after a service in Hagia Sophia, "knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth." Monks are everywhere, from city houses like the Stoudios to Mount Athos and the caves of Cappadocia, and the dying often take monastic vows so as to meet death as monks.
primer.byz_p_faith_jewish.title: The Jewish community
primer.byz_p_faith_jewish.text: You come from the Jewish community – in Constantinople, Thessalonica and other cities Jews live in their own quarters. Around 1168 the traveller Benjamin of Tudela counted 2,500 Jews in the City, Rabbanites and Karaites, many of them silk weavers and dyers in the Pera quarter. The law lets them pray in old synagogues but forbids building new ones, owning Christian slaves or serving the state. There have been persecutions too: Basil I and Romanos I tried to baptise Jews by force.
primer.byz_p_faith_catholic.title: The Latins
primer.byz_p_faith_catholic.text: You are a Latin, a Catholic – one of those the Romans call Franks. Most Latins are merchants from Venice, Genoa, Pisa and Amalfi: they have their own quarters on the Golden Horn, their own churches and privileges – since 1082 Venice has traded almost free of customs duty. The Romans envy their wealth and distrust their faith: in 1054 the pope's legates and Patriarch Michael Keroularios excommunicated each other, and Rome and Constantinople have been in schism ever since. In 1182 a mob in the City massacred the Latins.
primer.byz_p_faith_muslim.title: Muslims among the Romans
primer.byz_p_faith_muslim.text: You come from a Muslim family – there are few of them in the Roman empire. Constantinople has long had a mosque for Arab merchants and captives, and the emperor lets them pray. In Asia Minor Turks live alongside Greeks, and the line between them is blurred: they share a market, take service with each other and sometimes change faith. After 1453 everything is turned upside down: the City becomes the sultan's capital, and Muslims are its masters.
primer.byz_p_work.title: Land, guilds and gold
primer.byz_p_work.text: The economy rests on the land: nearly all Romans plough, herd sheep and press olives. In the City the guilds work – silk makers, bakers, butchers, money changers, notaries – and the Book of the Eparch (around 912) lays down strictly who may sell what, where and at what price. The main coin is the gold nomisma: 72 are struck from a pound of gold, and until the mid-eleventh century its purity holds. On every imported good the treasury takes the kommerkion – a tenth of its value.
primer.byz_p_place.title: Lands of the Romans
primer.byz_p_place.text: The Roman empire is sea and mountains: the Balkans, Asia Minor and the islands of the Aegean. Its cities stand on ancient sites, with old walls, aqueducts and forums under the rising domes of churches. People travel between them on old Roman roads and by ship – the sea is faster and safer. Around the cities lie olive groves, vineyards and wheat fields; sheep graze in the hills, and fortresses guard the passes against raids.
primer.byz_p_place_constantinople.title: The Queen of Cities
primer.byz_p_place_constantinople.text: Your city is Constantinople, the largest in Christendom: at its height, by various estimates, 200,000 to 400,000 people lived here. On the landward side it is guarded by the Theodosian Walls – nearly 6 kilometres of double walls with a moat – and above the roofs floats the dome of Hagia Sophia, over 55 metres high. On the main street, the Mese, silk and spices are sold; the Golden Horn harbour smells of tar and fish; and axe-bearing Varangians stand at the gates of the Great Palace.
primer.byz_p_place_thessalonica.title: City of Saint Demetrios
primer.byz_p_place_thessalonica.text: Thessalonica is the empire's second city. Its patron is Saint Demetrios: fragrant myrrh is believed to seep from his tomb in a huge basilica. In October, on his feast, a fair opens outside the walls, where – according to a twelfth-century account – cloth and goods arrive from Egypt, Italy, Bulgaria and the lands of the "Scythians". The city has seen dark days too: in 904 Arab pirates under Leo of Tripoli stormed it and carried off thousands into slavery, and in 1185 the Normans sacked it.
primer.byz_p_place_nicaea.title: City of councils
primer.byz_p_place_nicaea.text: Nicaea stands by Lake Askania behind walls with a hundred towers, built back in Roman times. Ecumenical councils met here in 325 and 787, and the townsfolk are proud of it. All around are olive groves, vineyards and mulberry trees, and Constantinople is a couple of days away across the straits. The city has changed hands more than once: around 1081 the Seljuks took it, in 1097 crusaders and Romans won it back, and after 1204 Nicaea became the capital of the Romans in exile.
primer.byz_p_place_trebizond.title: City on the "table"
primer.byz_p_place_trebizond.text: Trebizond stands on a rocky plateau between two ravines – hence its name, from the Greek trapeza, "table". Ships arrive from Crimea and Constantinople; from the south, over the mountains, come caravans from Tabriz with silk, spices and carpets. The city is famous for hazelnuts, wine and timber from the Pontic mountains, and high in the hills the monastery of the Virgin of Soumela clings to a sheer cliff. Rain and fog come more often here than anywhere else in the empire.
primer.byz_p_law.title: Roman law
primer.byz_p_law.text: The Romans' laws are Roman: under Leo VI the Wise the Basilika were compiled – sixty books of law in Greek. In the City the eparch judges, in the provinces the theme judges, and marriage and inheritance cases often go to church courts. Punishments are harsh and public: theft can cost a hand, grave crimes blinding or the loss of one's nose – thought more merciful than execution, since the criminal keeps time to repent. A church offers sanctuary, and few dare to violate it.
primer.byz_p_health.title: Doctors and saints
primer.byz_p_health.text: Roman physicians learn from Hippocrates and Galen, and monasteries run hospitals called xenones: the Pantokrator, founded by John II in 1136, had 50 beds, a separate ward for women and doctors working in shifts. The poor more often turn to the saints – to relics and healing springs like the Life-Giving Spring outside the City walls. Fevers, smallpox and malaria in the lowlands are dangerous, and from 1347 the plague. Historians estimate that perhaps one child in three does not live to five.
primer.byz_p_women.title: Wife and dowry
primer.byz_p_women.text: The law allows girls to marry at 12 and boys at 14, and matches are usually arranged by parents. The dowry is a wife's chief property, and her husband may not squander it: on his death it returns to her and the children. Noblewomen go out veiled and escorted by servants, while ordinary women sell in the market, spin, weave and bake. A widow may run her own affairs and act as guardian of her children – Roman women own shops, land and even ships.
primer.byz_p_women_noble.title: Noble Roman women
primer.byz_p_women_noble.text: A woman of your rank should not be seen by men outside the family: noble Roman women live in the women's quarters, the gynaikonitis, though in practice many run the household, the estates and their husband's business. Empresses have sometimes ruled in their own right – Irene, and in 1042 the sisters Zoe and Theodora. Anna Komnene, daughter of Alexios I, wrote the Alexiad, the history of her father's reign and one of the finest books of the age. Girls of noble houses learn to read, the Psalter, and sometimes Homer.
primer.byz_p_leisure.title: Feasts and pastimes
primer.byz_p_leisure.text: The Roman year follows the church calendar: Christmas, Epiphany with the blessing of the waters, Easter with its night service and processions, the feasts of patron saints. Holidays bring fairs, and in the streets perform mimes, acrobats and men with dancing bears – though the Church frowns on them. Men play dice and tavli, a game like backgammon, while nobles play tzykanion, a horseback polo that came from Persia. In the evenings people gather in taverns and baths.
primer.byz_p_leisure_constantinople.text: The City's great spectacle is the Hippodrome beside the Great Palace, holding by some estimates up to 100,000 spectators. Chariots race here, and the crowd cheers for the Blues or the Greens – once these factions raised riots; now they chant the emperor's praises at ceremonies. The basileus watches from his box, the kathisma, and this is where the crowd can shout a plea or a grievance at him. On the central spina stand an Egyptian obelisk and the bronze Serpent Column from Delphi.
primer.byz_p_knowledge.title: Roman scholars
primer.byz_p_knowledge.text: The Romans are among the most literate people of their time: in the cities many craftsmen and merchants can read, and an official cannot get by without good Greek. A child learns letters from the Psalter, then grammar, rhetoric and Homer. Patriarch Photios compiled the Myriobiblon, summaries of 279 books he had read, many of which will later be lost, and in the eleventh century Michael Psellos wrote about everything from philosophy to earthquakes. Books are written on parchment, and from the eleventh century on paper too.
primer.byz_p_war.title: Army and Greek fire
primer.byz_p_war.text: The Roman army is made up of theme soldiers, the stratiotai, who serve in return for land, and mercenaries: the City has its Varangian Guard – Scandinavians and Rus, and after 1066 Anglo-Saxons with huge axes. The great secret weapon is "Greek fire", a liquid sprayed from bronze siphons onto enemy ships; its recipe is so secret that it will eventually be lost. Still, the Romans prefer not to fight but to pay, negotiate and set enemies against each other – whole treatises are written on the art.
